claims.text: Interviewer-reported dyadic exposure: the interviewer discloses whether community or political-party representatives approached the interviewer (not the respondent) in connection with this fieldwork visit, so the observation is an interviewer's encounter with external mobilizers, not the respondent's own political contact.

evidence.quote: Were you approached by community and/or political party representatives?

claims.text: Affective threat is reported by the interviewer about the interviewer's own feeling during the interview; it records a felt state at interviewer grain, not an observed act or the respondent's fear.

evidence.quote: Did you feel threatened during the interview?

claims.text: Physically threatened is a distinct interviewer-side claim of bodily threat; it is separable from felt threat and from mere disruption, so a 'No' here does not negate a 'Yes' on felt threat.

evidence.quote: Were you physically threatened during the interview?

claims.text: Interviewer's retrospective characterization of the respondent's candor; the middle option is an explicit uncommitted judgment, not a mild version of adversarial candor, and refusal/don't-know are absent by design.

evidence.quote: honest, in between, or misleading?

claims.text: Forced-choice presidential legality item: respondents place themselves between presidential non-bindingness and presidential submission to laws and courts; the statement is conditional on the president's own belief, so the item measures rule-of-law stance, not an exposure.

evidence.quote: should not be bound by laws or court decisions that [he] thinks are wrong

claims.text: Military-intervention legitimacy item asks whether a hypothetical abusive incumbent entitles the armed forces to assume control; it registers a normative judgment conditioned on leader abuse, not a prediction of or exposure to a coup.

evidence.quote: take control of government when elected leaders abuse power

claims.text: Accountability-owner question for elected parliamentarians; the option list assigns ownership to executive, parliament/council, party, voters, or no one, so the observation contrasts who is normatively responsible for post-election performance rather than who in fact monitors.

evidence.quote: once elected, [members of Parliament] do their jobs?

claims.text: Parallel accountability-owner question for the president; the same owner categories but a different target allow comparing who is designated accountable for executive versus legislative performance without assuming the two share an answer domain.

evidence.quote: once elected, the [president] does [his] job?

claims.text: Hypothetical community-level anticipation of social sanction against a woman candidate; it records expected harassment, a projective judgment about others' likely behavior, not a report of witnessed harassment.

evidence.quote: criticized, called names, or harassed by others in the community

claims.text: Directive-demand item: respondents are asked whether government should do more, less, or about the right amount on women's rights and equality; the response is a judgment of government effort against a preferred level, not an assessment of achieved equality.

evidence.quote: should government and elected officials be doing more

claims.text: Single most-important women's-rights issue is a capped choice among six named issues plus an explicit no-issue option; the topology creates a forced prioritization, so picking one issue does not rate the others unimportant.

evidence.quote: which of the following issues related to women's rights

claims.text: Emergency-power justification item: acceptance of police/security enforcement of public health mandates is conditional on a declared health emergency and asks about temporary limitation of democratic freedoms, so agreement is not a general endorsement of policing.

evidence.quote: temporarily limit democracy or democratic freedoms

claims.text: Respondent's belief about who commissioned the survey; the option set spans survey producers, state, party, media, and metaphysical attribution, so the observation captures perceived sponsorship, not actual funder.

evidence.quote: Who do you think sent us to do this interview?

claims.text: Consent-to-recontact item records a stated willingness to be in follow-up surveys; it is a stated predisposition, with applicability restricted to respondents lacking a mobile number, and is not proof of future participation.

evidence.quote: Willing to participate in follow-up surveys

claims.text: The candor and threat items share interviewer-report grain but different referents (respondent's honesty vs interviewer's felt threat), so their joint use must not be read as a single interview-quality factor.

evidence.quote: Was he or she: honest
Did you feel threatened

claims.text: Both owner questions offer the executive as a possible owner of oversight for MPs, and the president as target; naming the executive for the legislature is structurally available, so divergent answers diagnose target-specific accountability reasoning rather than a single civic competence.

evidence.quote: The President / Executive
The Parliament / local government council

claims.text: Both fields are conditional and scope-restricted: Q63B is inapplicable where the COVID module was not fielded, and Q97 is asked of every respondent; comparing them would conflate a routed COVID judgment with an always-asked sponsorship belief.

evidence.quote: Not applicable (COV1=0, 8 or 9)
Refused to answer

Q106C.0: Interviewer reports no community or political-party representative approached the interviewer in connection with this fieldwork visit; this is a negative encounter report, not evidence that no mobilizer existed in the area.
Q106C.1: Interviewer reports being approached by community or party representatives; the two sources are merged into one category, so the kind of mobilizer cannot be recovered.

Q106D.0: Interviewer reports not having felt threatened; this displaces felt threat but does not report a physical incident or that the setting was safe for others.
Q106D.1: Interviewer reports a subjective sense of threat during the interview; no actor, wording, or physical act is specified.

Q106E.0: Interviewer reports no physical threat occurred; the negative covers bodily threat only and does not negate a separate felt-threat report.
Q106E.1: Interviewer reports that physical threat occurred during the interview; the identity of the threatening party is not captured.

Q109F.1: Interviewer characterizes the respondent as candid in answering; this is an interviewer evaluation, not a verified truthfulness finding.
Q109F.2: Interviewer places the respondent between candid and misleading; an explicit uncommitted middle judgment, not low candor.
Q109F.3: Interviewer characterizes the respondent as misleading; this is a negative interviewer impression about candor, distinct from refusing or not knowing.

inquiries.question: Among interviews where the interviewer reports felt or physical threat, does the respondent's attributed sponsorship (state, party, or Afrobarometer/partner) co-vary with the threat report in a way that would distinguish a real pressure environment from a misattribution or random interviewer distress?
inquiries.alternatives: If threat reports concentrate where sponsorship is attributed to the state or a party, this supports an environment-of-pressure reading; if threat reports are flat across sponsor categories or concentrate among Afrobarometer-attributors, it supports interviewer-level or misattribution readings and defeats the pressure interpretation.
inquiries.ceiling: Interviewer-clustered data and country non-administration of Q63B-style routes are not qualified here; nothing on actual intimidation causation, and no numerics are asserted.
inquiries.route: S04 existing observation-scope and asked-eligible RAW owner; only after source route, design and roles qualified.

inquiries.question: Does anticipated harassment of a woman candidate select a different women's-rights priority and a different demand direction than a general-expansion stance, i.e., are hostile-environment perceivers more likely to name gender-based violence and demand more government action than those who expect little sanction?
inquiries.alternatives: If high anticipated sanction pairs with gender-based-violence priority and more-government demand, this supports a threat-to-priority linkage; if high-sanction respondents name structural issues (pay, property) or prefer the status quo, the sanction-expectation and policy-preference accounts are rival readings.
inquiries.ceiling: Cross-sectional metadata only; priority is capped-choice so nonselection does not imply low importance, and nothing establishes that expectations cause demand.
inquiries.route: S04 existing observation-scope and asked-eligible RAW owner; only after source route, design and roles qualified.

inquiries.question: Do respondents who assign legislative oversight to the executive also endorse presidential non-bindingness or conditional military takeover, indicating an executive-centered accountability frame, or do the two items dissociate?
inquiries.alternatives: A coherent executive-centered configuration (executive-owned oversight plus presidential latitude plus intervention legitimacy) supports a single frame; dissociation would show that owner designation about MPs is not a proxy for authoritarian legality and would defeat that transfer.
inquiries.ceiling: Owner categories are nominal with merged party/voter options; no causal inference and no claim that owner answers predict behavior.
inquiries.route: S04 existing observation-scope and asked-eligible RAW owner; only after source route, design and roles qualified.

nominations.reason: Presence of listeners during the interview may condition the meaning of interviewer threat and sponsor reports; retrieval needed before any joint is asserted.
Respondent consultation with others could mediate candor judgments; exact labels required before linking to Q109F.
Interviewer-perceived influence on answers is adjacent to the candor item; retrieval would clarify whether these are distinct response acts.
Companion emergency-power measure (media censorship) needed to test whether Q63B endorsement is enforcement-specific or generalized emergency acceptance.
Government preparedness for future emergencies may rival the emergency-legitimacy reading; exact domain needed before any joint.
Mobile-phone ownership conditions the Q98A applicability flag; retrieval would test whether the recontact scope state is materially patterned.
Internet access on the phone may refine the recontact route; unverified until retrieved.
Respondent race/ethnicity context could condition interviewer threat and sponsor attribution; retrieval needed before interpretation.
Interviewer gender may mediate threat reports and candor judgments; retrieval needed to test the interviewer-grain reading.
Interviewer rural/urban origin could condition mobility and safety reports; exact labels required.
PSU/EA urban-rural distinction is a plausible scope condition for both threat and sponsorship beliefs; exact labels required.
Sponsorship beliefs about the state and emergency mandates are time-sensitive; interview date would locate the observations.
Verbatim interviewer comment may record the substance behind refusal and threat codes; retrieval needed, no interpretation now.

holds.missing: Fieldwork timing, interviewer identity and clustering, region, and any record of what a threat consisted of.
holds.why: Without these, the interviewer-grain encounter items cannot be read as environment indicators or as interviewer distress; the direction of any relation remains unidentified.

holds.missing: Verified full-wave administration since the stems carry country-specific placeholders and Q28 carries a country non-asked code.
holds.why: Cross-country comparability of the forced-choice legality and intervention items cannot be established from blended stem metadata alone.

holds.missing: Confirmation of whether the two owner questions were co-administered in the same wave and country, since Q48A carries a country-date non-asked code.
holds.why: A same-respondent comparison of presidential versus legislative oversight attribution presupposes joint administration that this metadata does not establish.

holds.missing: The COV1 eligibility variable that routes Q63B to not applicable.
holds.why: The denominator of emergency-justification responses and any comparison with other emergency items cannot be fixed without the routing record.

holds.missing: Whether recontact willingness is conditioned on sponsor belief and on mobile availability across countries.
holds.why: The recontact scope state cannot be interpreted as general unwillingness versus inapplicability without cell-level evidence not present here.
